hedge_exemplars.value: If measured nocturnal temperature differences correlate more strongly with anthropogenic heat flux than with sky view factor, this mechanism is insufficient.
If reducing anthropogenic emissions does not decrease the nocturnal UHI gap in controlled studies, this mechanism is insufficient.
If the nocturnal UHI gap does not scale with impervious surface fraction across cities, thermal admittance alone is insufficient.
If the UHI is large even on windy nights in some cities, wind sheltering is insufficient.

The target's claim that the cross-city nocturnal UHI gap depends 'mainly on sky view factor' presents sky view as the single dominant cross-city modulator, but the problem asks for 'what single mechanism best explains why that night-time gap is larger in some cities than in others.' Sky view factor

The target answers the 'single mechanism best explains why the gap is larger in some cities' question with anthropogenic heat flux, but this is empirically the weaker cross-city predictor. The dominant, widely-cited cross-city modulator of nocturnal UHI intensity is urban geometry / sky-view factor

The target invokes 'longwave radiative cooling' and 'lower emissivity' as its core mechanism, claiming that lower emissivity 'can further slow radiative loss.'
